item.title: PSPs, high-risk processors, and offshore layers
item.lead: The dossier describes international payment structures as a form of jurisdictional opportunism: various links each have a limited view of the whole.

blocks.text: The source geographically separates payment processors, holdings, and operational agencies. The examples used mention, among others, Europe, the United States, Cyprus, Delaware, and Dubai. The analytical point is not that every named jurisdiction would be suspicious, but that international dispersion can fragment responsibility.

The source suggests that high-risk payment processors can play a role when a sector experiences many chargebacks, sensitive content, or complex consumer disputes. The legal assessment of this is context-dependent. For this dossier, it primarily means that the payment layer should not be treated as a neutral technical infrastructure, but as a place where compliance, risk, and business choices converge.

A financial investigation should therefore ask who the merchant of record is, who the account holder is, which entity receives the payout, under what conditions the PSP operates, and which KYC/AML obligations apply. The dossier formulates these questions implicitly; this edition makes them more explicit as a research agenda.

The offshore structure in the source is a mechanism of opacity. This is a hypothesis that only becomes robust when company registers, shareholder documents, service agreements, and payment data can actually be linked to each other.

rows: Who pays, how often, and for what?

blocks.text: PSP / platform How is payment made and disbursed? Merchant files, payout data, KYC/AML
Agency / holding Who receives and controls the proceeds? Register data, contracts, bank records
Intermediate entity Why does the intermediate layer exist? UBO, invoice, and service documents
